about: Per-field provenance for compounds.json. availability records what is known about where a value came from; origin records how it came to hold the value it does. They are independent: a value can be asserted with its basis unrecorded. Verifying a stored value against a formula does not make its origin derived -- only authorship does. See docs/DATA_SOURCES.md.

availability.known: The basis for this value is recorded here.
availability.unknown: A basis exists but has not been established.
availability.not_recorded: A basis existed when the value was entered and was not written down. A historical fact about this table, not a statement about the literature.
availability.not_applicable: The field is conceptually inapplicable to this entry.

origin.derived: Computed here from a stated expression and standard. Requires formula, expression, standard and standard_version.
origin.cited: Taken from a identified publication. Requires a citation identifier.
origin.asserted: Recorded as a value with no basis captured. May coexist with availability not_recorded.
origin.corrected: The value was already here and was repaired. Records what it was, what was changed and what established the new reading. Distinct from derived, which claims the value was authored here.

investigation.question: Do the bundled compounds have counterparts in the TPP parameter series?
scope: Tanuma, Powell & Penn, Surf. Interface Anal. 17, 927 (1991)
Shinotsuka et al., Surf. Interface Anal. 51, 427 (2019)
Shinotsuka et al., Surf. Interface Anal. 54, 534 (2022)
investigation.result: Five of the eleven compounds appear. Al2O3, GaAs, SiC and SiO2 are in both the 1991 and the 2019 sets, whose parameters differ from each other as well as from the bundled ones (Al2O3 Eg is 9.0 in 1991 and 8.63 in 2019 against 7.6 here); both are recorded under comparisons. Si3N4 is in the 1991 set only -- the 2019 study dropped it and LiF for sum-rule errors. TiO2, HfO2, ZrO2, Ta2O5, SrTiO3 and GeO2 appear in none of the three.
investigation.limits: Three parts of a series running to at least Part XIII were read. Later parts have not been surveyed, so an absence here is not an absence from the series.

investigation.question: Can SESSA (NIST SRD 100) supply an independently sourced density or band gap for the six compounds with no TPP counterpart?
scope: SESSA v2.2.2 bundled databases, read locally
investigation.result: No. SESSA has no band-gap database outside its 100-entry TPP table, and none of the six is in that table. Its compound density table carries no per-entry source, and its HfO2 density is 9.68 -- the value already bundled here, so not an independent check. It did establish the GeO2 and TiO2 phase ambiguities recorded above.
investigation.limits: Read-only inspection of the shipped databases. SESSA was not run. Its own Si3N4 row attributes parameters to the 2019 paper, which states that it excluded Si3N4, so that attribution is not usable.

investigation.question: Should the bundled parameters for the five compounds with published counterparts be replaced by those published values?
scope: Tanuma, Powell & Penn, Surf. Interface Anal. 21, 165 (1994), p. 170 -- the paper that introduces TPP-2M, which is the formula implemented here
investigation.result: No blanket replacement on grounds of consistency with the TPP-2M fit: that argument selects neither generation. It is a statement about a blanket choice only, and leaves open any future change to an individual entry made on its own primary source or on an explicit phase specification. The argument for preferring the 1991 parameters was that a formula should be fed the parameter set it was fitted on; the 1994 paper refutes it. On p. 170 it states that the modified expression for beta -- the one change TPP-2M makes to TPP-2 -- was derived from the 27 elements and the 14 organic compounds, and that 'the IMFPs for the group of 15 inorganic compounds have been excluded from this analysis because the optical data on which their IMFPs are based are much less reliable than for the other two groups of materials'. Neither generation was in the fit, so neither is privileged by it, and adopting one wholesale on that basis would be a preference rather than a correction.
investigation.effect_size: For scale, not as the argument. Substituting either published set moves lambda by at most 3.8% at 1 keV (Al2O3 against the 1991 set, relative to the bundled value) and 7.6% at 50 eV -- the differences grow toward low energy, so a single-energy figure understates them. The right yardstick is not the 18.9% group average but the per-compound RMS deviations the same paper tabulates (Table 8, p. 173): SiC 3.2, SiO2 3.6, Si3N4 11.8, Al2O3 15.3, GaAs 39.6. Against those, the parameter-induced differences are smaller but not negligible: about 3x below the formula's own error for SiC and SiO2 -- the two with the smallest RMS in that table. The paper attributes the inorganic deviations to limitations of the optical data as a group; it states no per-material judgement of optical-data quality, and none is claimed here.
investigation.limits: This settles a blanket replacement, and nothing more. It is NOT a finding that every bundled value is as good as its published counterpart. Al2O3's Eg of 7.6 eV differs from both published figures (8.63 and 9.0) and has no recorded basis; a case for changing one value on its own evidence remains open and would need its own citation. The SiC entry is still unlabelled, and its Eg implies a different polytype from its published counterparts -- 3.26 eV is the 4H figure, the tables carry the cubic 3C 2.31 -- while its density discriminates no polytype, so adopting the cubic figures to resolve it would silently redefine what the name SiC means here. Phase-specific entries are the better route to that and were not attempted. Al2O3's density (3.95 against 3.97 in both published sets) is likewise unrecorded, though the band gap dominates the difference.
